   <description>The French government's budget proposal includes a €1.2 billion increase in funding for the National Education Ministry, as France grapples with one of the highest public deficits in the eurozone.</description>

   <title>Russia funnels nearly half its budget into defence, cutting social spending</title>
   <link>https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/13/russia-funnels-nearly-half-its-budget-into-defence-cutting-social-spending</link>
   <guid>https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/13/russia-funnels-nearly-half-its-budget-into-defence-cutting-social-spending</guid>
   <pubDate>Tue, 13 Oct 2026 17:05:02 +0200</pubDate>
   <description>Russia’s 2027 draft budget allocates a record share to defence and security, as regions quietly divert funds for foster children and orphans to war payments and “coffin money” for soldiers’ families is cut by up to 95% in some areas.</description>

   <title>Women with autoimmune diseases face longer waits and more misdiagnoses than men</title>

   <pubDate>Tue, 13 Oct 2026 16:55:18 +0200</pubDate>
   <description>Women are significantly more likely than men to face prolonged delays and have physical autoimmune symptoms dismissed as psychological conditions, such as anxiety or depression, a study has found.</description>

      <description><p>Committee recognises work of South African who chaired UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza</p><p></p><p>The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2025/sep/16/israel-committed-genocide-in-gaza-says-un-inquiry">that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza</a>.</p><p>The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/09/navanethem-navi-pillay-wins-nobel-peace-prize">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Isaias strengthens to become first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 season</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/09/isaias-strengthens-first-atlantic-hurricane-2026</link>
      <description><p>Storm expected to make landfall on US’s northern Gulf coast with risk of flash floods and isolated river flooding</p><p>Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb. It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).</p><p>As a result of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/sep/26/what-is-el-nino-causes-can-we-reduce-risks">the strong El Niño</a>, it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/09/isaias-strengthens-first-atlantic-hurricane-2026">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2026/oct/09/egypt-six-journalists-matsadaash-protest-over-detentions</link>
      <description><p>Matsadaash staff allege torture and forced confessions after being held on charges of working for Muslim Brotherhood</p><p>Egyptian journalists are planning a new protest in Cairo this weekend after <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/04/egyptian-journalist-faces-terrorism-charges-entire-newsroom-detained-matsadaash-press-freedom">six colleagues were charged with terrorism offences</a> amid allegations they had been tortured in police detention.</p><p>Last week, Egyptian authorities arrested the journalists, from the independent factchecking and investigative platform Matsadaash, accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and producing false news on behalf of the outlawed <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/muslim-brotherhood">Muslim Brotherhood</a>.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2026/oct/09/egypt-six-journalists-matsadaash-protest-over-detentions">Continue reading...</a></description>

News from the US, Europe, Asia Pacific, Africa, Middle East, America</description><link>https://www.france24.com/en/</link><lastBuildDate>Tue, 13 Oct 2026 16:05:44 GMT</lastBuildDate><atom:link href="https://www.france24.com/en/rss" rel="self" type="application/rss+xml"/><item><category></category><title>France: Student anger rages as tear gas and fires hit Paris</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/france-student-anger-rages-as-tear-gas-and-fires-hit-paris</link><description>
Around 480,000 people took part in nationwide student demonstrations across France on Tuesday, according to student and school unions, up from the previous week’s mobilisation. In Paris, the demonstration ended with tear gas and fires, as tensions escalated. Claire Paccalin has the latest.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/c583610a-c71d-11f1-953b-29a2e29ae696/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261013-173108-173500-CS.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/c583610a-c71d-11f1-953b-29a2e29ae696/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261013-173108-173500-CS.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">ca6d2ade-c71d-11f1-a902-cb0f39029e6a</guid><pubDate>Tue, 13 Oct 2026 16:03:37 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>From Paris to Marseille, high school protests continue across France</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/video/20261013-from-paris-to-marseille-high-school-protests-continue-across-france</link><description>
Student protests continue across France, with marches taking place in cities including Lille and Marseille while pupils in Paris stage fresh school blockades using wheelie bins. Demonstrators are calling for better learning conditions, saying government measures announced so far have failed to address their concerns. 
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/3a618d84-c71a-11f1-96ba-e362370cce2e/w:1024/p:16x9/minimanif.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/3a618d84-c71a-11f1-96ba-e362370cce2e/w:1024/p:16x9/minimanif.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">5322f998-c71a-11f1-aadf-31245b2721cf</guid><pubDate>Tue, 13 Oct 2026 15:40:53 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>In Kenya, recycled plastic gets a second life as chess pieces</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/in-kenya-recycled-plastic-gets-a-second-life-as-chess-pieces</link><description>
In Nairobi, a project is helping children develop focus, patience and critical thinking through chess, using pieces made from recycled plastic waste.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/4a99973e-c718-11f1-9dfa-e362370cce2e/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261012-225312-225439-CS.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/4a99973e-c718-11f1-9dfa-e362370cce2e/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261012-225312-225439-CS.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">4fa1c26a-c718-11f1-90b1-1b19ca1118fa</guid><pubDate>Tue, 13 Oct 2026 15:28:46 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item><item><category>France in focus</category><title>Broken children: France confronts crisis of sexual violence against minors</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/france-in-focus/20261013-broken-children-france-confronts-crisis-of-sexual-violence-against-minors</link><description>
In France, a new "comprehensive law" aims to strengthen preventative measures, the judicial process and support for child victims of sexual violence. Yet advocacy groups, lawyers, and healthcare professionals point out that the legislation has numerous shortcomings. We take a closer look in this edition of France in Focus. Warning: viewers may find parts of this report disturbing.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/075a50da-c6d7-11f1-b929-3774aeac812a/w:1024/p:16x9/PIC-2-CEF-VIOLENCES-SEXUELLES-MINEURS-2.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/075a50da-c6d7-11f1-b929-3774aeac812a/w:1024/p:16x9/PIC-2-CEF-VIOLENCES-SEXUELLES-MINEURS-2.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">376f86c2-c6dd-11f1-af70-75b97fc69acf</guid><pubDate>Tue, 13 Oct 2026 15:24:00 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>Aurore Cloé DUPUIS</dc:creator></item><item><category></category><title>French youth demand answers as education protests enter third week</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/french-youth-demand-answers-as-education-protests-enter-third-week</link><description>
French students have continued nationwide protests for a third week, demanding more funding for education, better teaching conditions and more staff. The government’s plan to recruit 3,000 substitute teachers has failed to satisfy demonstrators, who are calling for an additional €10 billion in education spending. Backed by teachers and unions, protesters warn the mobilisation will continue as the government prepares budget cuts.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/acc0217e-c715-11f1-9f1c-29a2e29ae696/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261013-163631-163805-CS.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/acc0217e-c715-11f1-9f1c-29a2e29ae696/w:1024/p:16x9/EN-20261013-163631-163805-CS.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">b1d7c69e-c715-11f1-86ad-e9e3444e4d54</guid><pubDate>Tue, 13 Oct 2026 15:18:00 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>FRANCE24</dc:creator></item></channel></rss>

<![CDATA[ Latest from Space.com ]]> https://www.space.com/feeds.xml Tue, 13 Oct 2026 16:00:00 +0000 en <![CDATA[ 2 spacecraft in orbit and 8 more coming soon: Varda has big plans for in-space manufacturing ]]> Reentry and orbital-manufacturing provider Varda Space Industries is operating two spacecraft in orbit right now, with another expected to launch "in the coming days" and seven more next year.

The Los Angeles-area startup, which bills itself as one of just two companies that can currently do commercial reentry from space, successfully launched its latest two refrigerator-sized spacecraft aboard SpaceX's Transporter-18 rideshare mission on Oct. 1.

"It's humanity's first time launching multiple commercial reentry vehicles simultaneously," Varda CEO Will Bruey told Space.com on Tuesday (Oct. 7) of the Transporter-18 launch.

The payloads on the Transporter-18 Varda craft ranged from pharmaceuticals to demo navigation systems to exterior thermal-protection materials. The company bills its spacecraft as mini-factories, which can host the orbital production of valuable goods such as pharmaceuticals and then bring them safely down to Earth.

Another Varda vehicle is scheduled to follow them into space later this month. Assuming the third spacecraft launches nominally, all three will come down before Christmas in the Koonibba Test Range in the South Australian Outback, through coordination with Varda's long-time space-mission service provider, Southern Launch. And things are scheduled to ramp up quickly: Varda aims to fly seven more missions in 2027: two in Quarter 1 (Q1), two in Q2 and three in Q3 (the latter three being all on the same rocket).

"As we scale up, we care about our ability to fly and fly regularly," Bruey said, emphasizing that the company is now treating its missions less as one-offs and more as a series. "It is, first and foremost, taking that unique [spacecraft] technology and moving into a fleet mentality, rather than a space mission mentality."

Like any startup finding its footing, Varda's challenges in the coming months will be scaling safely and efficiently. But the company says it is well-capitalized to do so, and has a big hiring campaign underway. It also has been spending money on slight upgrades and improvements to its vehicles, as well as mission operations and other infrastructure to run several missions at the same time, with more funds having just arrived.

In September, Varda announced it had raised $251 million in "Series D" investment funding and will be hiring 100 people by the end of 2027, boosting its current 286-employee base by more than a third. Most of the employees work out of El Segundo, California, with a few in sales offices in Washington, D.C. and Huntsville, Alabama (where U.S. Space Command is gradually moving, along with some defense contractors, from Colorado Springs).

In the further future, Bruey said, the goal is to fly Varda vehicles into space daily, using a "standardized product" that would be put together on an assembly line. But to get to that point, like other companies in the industry, Varda will need to get through an anticipated rocket shortage beginning in about 2029.

SpaceX is by far the most active launcher these days, and it has been the dominant provider for companies like Varda via its Transporter and Bandwagon rideshare programs. But SpaceX is readying to retire its Falcon 9 rocket as it transitions more resources into Starship, the fully reusable megarocket the company sees as its workhorse of the future. Media reports suggest that SpaceX is pretty much out of capacity for Falcon 9 rockets flying through the end of service in 2028 or 2029, although slots are still available through third-party bookers.

There are a slew of newer rockets under production (such as Blue Origin's New Glenn and Relativity Space's Terran R), though they are far less mature and in some cases, even unflown. This is creating uncertainty about how much capacity there will be in the industry in the short term, but Varda said it is planning well ahead for that moment — and so too are its customers.

"We're stacked with launches from now through that 2029 time frame," Bruey said. The company's current generation of vehicles is "launch-agnostic," although the next generation is aiming to be even more so to nab opportunities from small rockets up to Starship.

The company said that, as long as Varda and its customers have access to microgravity, the shipping methodology — much like shipping on Earth — should not matter, and Varda aims to make the experience that seamless for its customers. But in the meantime, the company says it will fly as much as possible and (like everyone else) do what it can to secure slots on launching rockets after Falcon 9 retires.

]]> <![CDATA[ ‘Space Gal’ Emily Calandrelli launches into the Marvel Universe this week on Disney Jr.'s 'Iron Man' series (exclusive) ]]>

"The Space Gal" is blasting off onto her next adventure to promote STEM education with out-of-this-world content.

Science communicator and citizen astronaut Emily Calandrelli, better known to millions of social media followers as "The Space Gal," is bringing her real-world spaceflight experience to the Marvel universe. Calandrelli is lending her voice to an upcoming episode of Disney Jr.'s animated series, "Marvel's Iron Man and his Awesome Friends."

She is stepping into the role of a character called Astronaut Amy in the episode "The Iron Friends in Space," offering another opportunity for Calandrelli to share her enthusiasm for space with younger audiences.

Calandrelli is an engineer, author and television host whose career has focused on making complex scientific concepts engaging and accessible. Growing from her online presence as @TheSpaceGal, Calandrelli has produced numerous educational videos, books and television appearances, including a role on the Netflix "Bill Nye the Science Guy" revival series, "Bill Nye Saves the World."

In a preview clip provided exclusively to Space.com by Disney, Calandrelli's character is welcomed by Tony Stark, Riri Williams, Amadeus Cho and Vision as they explore a moon-themed museum display. The exhibit features a holographic model of the moon and other space-themed artifacts, providing a backdrop for Astronaut Amy to share information about space and lunar exploration.

The show follows younger versions of Stark and others from Marvel's familiar superhero roster, as they navigate conflicts that are scaled down from the franchise's world-ending blockbuster emergencies to more age-appropriate problem-solving and teamwork-building storylines.

Calandrelli's cameo puts her alongside characters already rich in their storylines with backgrounds in science and technology, like Stark and Williams, known by their alter egos Iron Man and Ironheart, both of whose superhero identities revolve around the mastery of sophisticated technology and engineering. And while Astronaut Amy and her super co-stars live in Marvel's fictional universe, Calandrelli's inclusion in the episode creates the opportunity to introduce some real-life scientific concepts.

Her appearance also comes as Disney prepares to expand the animated series to include a larger ensemble. Beginning next summer, the show will evolve into "Marvel's Avengers: Mightiest Friends", and bring additional characters into the fold, including Captain America, Hulk, Black Panther, Black Widow and Thor, according to Disney. For Calandrelli, the role represents another extension of a career dedicated to making space exploration relatable and exciting for the next generation.

In November 2024, Calandrelli became the 100th woman to reach space when she launched aboard Blue Origin's New Shepard rocket on the company's NS-28 suborbital mission. The flight carried her above the Kármán line, the internationally recognized boundary of space, and gave her several minutes of weightlessness before the capsule and its crew returned to Earth.

Calandrelli isn't the first real-life astronaut to lend her voice to the Marvel universe. Former NASA astronaut and the first Black woman in space Mae Jemison guest-starred in Disney's "Marvel's Moon Girl and Devil Dinosaur" in March 2023. Jemison voiced a fictional app called Skipster, created by the show's young superhero and scientific prodigy, Lunella Lafayette. Another space traveler, citizen astronaut Kellie Gerardi, also just announced over the weekend (Oct. 12) her cast credit in the upcoming movie "Hexed", from Disney's Animation Studios.

Viewers can catch the upcoming episode of "Marvel's Iron Man and his Awesome Friends," titled, "The Iron Friends in Space," during its Disney Jr. premiere on Oct. 14 or streaming on Disney+ beginning Oct. 28.

]]> <![CDATA[ NASA's Perseverance Mars rover breaks interplanetary driving record — and it's far from done ]]> In a milestone achievement, NASA's Perseverance Mars rover has broken the record for most miles driven on a world beyond Earth.

On Oct. 11, Perseverance hit 28.10 miles (45.22 kilometers) traveled on Mars, breaking the record previously held by NASA's Opportunity rover which went 28.06 miles (45.16 km). It took Oppy 14 years to cover all that ground; Perseverance, by contrast, has been on Mars for just 5.5 years.

The new record is far from the end of Perseverance's journey, however; the mission team thinks the rover could eventually more than double the distance it's already traveled.

"Our original design was only planned to last for [about] 20 kilometers of driving," Mark Maimone, a rover driver at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California, told Space.com.

"We've more than doubled that already … and we're looking really good to go for up to 100 kilometers total," added Maimone, who works as a designated principal in autonomous planetary rover navigation on Perseverance and helped to develop the autonomous driving systems on NASA's previous Mars rovers.

"So we could double what we've done so far," he said. "And we have great expectations that [Perseverance] can continue its mission of exploring and collecting really useful and beneficial samples that will tell us so much more about the history of Mars."

Indeed, Perseverance remains in great shape, mission team members stressed.

"We are very fortunate that all of Perseverance's original capabilities are more or less intact, especially for the science instruments," JPL's Vivian Sun, the mission's deputy project scientist, told Space.com.

Perseverance landed on the floor of Mars' 28-mile-wide (46 km) Jezero Crater in February 2021. It was far from the first robot to traverse the planet's surface; the Perseverance team built on years of experience with the Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity and Curiosity rovers.

Through the triumphs and missteps of these previous craft, NASA learned how to better explore another planet with a rover operated from millions of miles away. Perseverance saw massive improvements made to everything from its specialty wheels to its autonomous driving system and onboard tools and instruments.

This "could not have been done without the previous missions that we've sent to Mars," Sun said.

"Five years later [after landing], we're definitely a very well oiled machine," she added. "There's a lot of technical advancements on Perseverance that are the result of many people, many engineers, working on this new technology year after year for decades now."

And, according to both Sun and Maimone, this teamwork is the real secret behind Perseverance's endurance and success.

"The magic sauce for our operations team is how cohesively we work together," Sun said. The engineers, rover drivers and science team all work together and keep each other's work in mind as they make decisions on everything from driving speed to science targets, she added.

"I'm just super appreciative of all the people that have and still work on the mission. They're really what makes the mission special," Sun said.

What's next for Perseverance

As the team mentioned, Perseverance is nowhere near done on Mars. The rover could keep driving for many more miles on the Red Planet, and the scientists and engineers at NASA have big plans and high hopes for its future.

"We are currently planning to continue down south on the crater rim," Sun said. "There's a whole diversity of different rocks along this crater rim going south that we want to investigate and figure out how it indicates conditions from early Mars."

Jezero is a giant crater created by an impact from an asteroid or comet billions of years ago. Perseverance's work has shown that Jezero hosted a lake for long stretches billions of years ago. Scientists are therefore eager to continue exploring the site, searching for clues about what the planet looked like in the ancient past, and if it could have possibly hosted life.

"There are huge chunks of pre-Jezero crust that were embedded in the stratigraphy or got thrown up by the impact, and they're now incorporated onto the crater rim," Sun said. "These are our chance to probe like really old rocks that don't really exist in any other form on the surface anymore."

As part of Perseverance's next steps south on the crater rim, the team is heading toward an area called "Rainbow Falls."

Sun said that the Rainbow Falls area is thought to have kaolinite, a clay mineral that forms when water interacts with rock. By studying these types of minerals, mission scientists might be able to get a better idea of the conditions on Mars all of those billions of years ago, when water filled Jezero Crater.

"Whenever we are looking at clay minerals, I think the question of habitability and the search for potential biosignatures is always on the table," Sun said. "So that is very much the case when we get to Rainbow Falls, or even when we see kaolinite."

]]> <![CDATA[ Astronaut captures mesmerizing auroras with iPhone from ISS | Space photo of the day for Oct. 13, 2026 ]]>

NASA astronaut Anil Menon captured a gorgeous view of the northern lights dancing over the night side of Earth from the International Space Station on Oct. 10 using an iPhone camera.

What is it?

Menon's photo reveals spectacular pink, purple and red auroras glowing in Earth's upper atmosphere above a sparse dappling of city lights, subtly blurred by the motion of the orbital spacecraft over the course of the exposure.

Bright stars glimmer between the solar panels and outer hulls of the ISS and visiting spacecraft, painted purple by the auroral display. "Flying through is rare and amazing," Menon wrote in a separate aurora video he posted to X on Oct. 10. "You can see the lights on the outside of [the] station reflecting back like Christmas LEDs. It's definitely more immersive."

Why is it amazing?

Menon captured the auroras during a period of heightened geomagnetic activity, after several coronal mass ejections (CMEs) struck Earth's magnetic field, triggering geomagnetic storms ranging from minor (G1) to strong (G3) over the weekend.

During geomagnetic storms, more charged particles are accelerated along Earth's magnetic field lines toward the polar regions, where they collide with gases in the upper atmosphere; they excite them, causing them to release energy as light and producing spectacular auroral displays.

The blue-purple colors seen in Menon's image are largely produced by nitrogen at altitudes of around 60-120 miles (100-200 kilometers) , while the red hue comes from oxygen atoms higher up, typically above 125 miles (200 kilometers).

The photo is particularly impressive because it was captured on an iPhone camera, as opposed to the more traditional Nikon cameras that astronauts sometimes use to capture Earth during their time aboard the ISS.

Smartphone astrophotography has become increasingly popular over recent years, with some models now featuring bespoke modes for capturing the night sky. iPhones were even used by the astronauts of the Artemis 2 mission to document their historic flyby of the moon earlier this year!

Interested in capturing your own images of the night sky using your mobile phone? Then be sure to check out our guide to photographing stars, the moon and the Milky Way with nothing but your smartphone camera.

]]> <![CDATA[ The great Halley's Comet disappointment of 1986 — and the discoveries that changed astronomy forever ]]> This year, 2026, marks the 40th anniversary of the most recent appearance of Halley's Comet, the most famous comet in the solar system.

Roughly every 76 years, Halley punctuates history like an exclamation mark in the night sky. As writer Guy Ottewell has said, it is the "wildest of the tame comets."

It is a tame comet because it can be anticipated. It is wild because it is still fresh and bright; the brightest of all the recurring comets. It is the only one that periodically becomes conspicuous to the naked eye.

Halley through history

Before 1986, Halley had been seen and recorded on 29 occasions. In A.D. 66, observers described it as a sword in the skies above Jerusalem. In 1066, its image was woven into the strip of linen now known as the Bayeux Tapestry, where an agitated crowd of Saxons points toward a fiery comet we know to be Halley. In 1301, the Florentine painter Giotto di Bondone witnessed the comet and was so impressed that, a few years later, he depicted a comet as the star that led the Magi to Bethlehem in one of his magnificent frescoes in Padua's Scrovegni Chapel.

More recently, Halley passed unusually close to Earth in 1910. As the 1986 return approached, people who remembered that earlier appearance likely told their children and grandchildren about being awakened before dawn and taken outside to see a huge, ghostly, gleaming object in the sky.

Halley's earlier appearances suggested that each return to the inner solar system might produce a magnificent display. Little wonder, then, that the public expected great things in 1986.

The great disappointment of 1986

Halley's 1986 return therefore became two very different stories: a frustrating spectacle for much of the public and an unprecedented scientific opportunity for astronomers.

But for many who saw it — or tried to — in 1986, Halley is remembered as a tremendous disappointment. Heavily promoted as the most anticipated celestial event of the second half of the 20th century, the comet proved to be an underwhelming sight that belied promises of a spectacle never to be seen again.

In all fairness, Halley's subpar performance was not unexpected. During the mid-1970's, comet experts had warned that the comet would likely disappoint much of the general public. Despite that, the comet's impending arrival was accompanied by a frenzy of T-shirts, commemorative comet medals, bumper stickers, and specially marketed telescopes. Halley logos could be found on warm-up jackets, cocktail glasses, cereal boxes, and just about everything in sight. Caught up in the grip of Halley-mania, the mainstream media emphasized that the comet would be a "once-in-a-lifetime spectacle."

One of the main problems for many trying to see the comet that year was light pollution; the total outdoor illumination in the United States had increased tremendously since Halley's previous visit in 1910. Indeed, in 1986, many of the largest cities were bathed in permanent twilight, with only the brightest stars and planets visible from near city centers and with astronomically unacceptable conditions up to 50 miles (80 km) away.

On the evening of Jan. 11, in New York City, thousands gathered at four city parks to get a view of Halley's Comet. Mayor Ed Koch and Parks Commissioner Henry J. Stern arranged to have the lights turned off at four public parks, where telescopes were set up. The comet itself was not overly impressive, but many were still happy just to get a glimpse of it. As Stern put it: "Those who came for the comet saw the comet — the cynics didn't — but it was there."

When Halley passed through perihelion — its closest point to the sun — on Feb. 9, it lay on the far side of the sun as viewed from Earth and was hidden in the solar glare. During much of March, it brightened only to third magnitude and displayed a tail about a dozen degrees long, merely one-tenth the extent of its 1910 splendor. At the same time, it moved southward through the stars of Sagittarius, Scorpius, and Centaurus. Because those constellations appear low above the southern horizon, the comet was difficult to see from Canada, Europe, and the northern United States.

The 1986 apparition was, in fact, described as the comet's worst in 2,000 years. And as one would expect, the public wasn't impressed. Having read that he'd need binoculars and a star map just to find the comet, taxi driver David A. Gittelman penned a New York Times opinion piece entitled "Who Cares About Halley's Comet Anyway?" In it he wrote:

"I was devastated. How could such an injustice be allowed to prevail? All my life I'd been waiting — all my life. What happened to the cosmic leviathan of my childhood dreams?"

What happened was that at its closest approach to Earth on April 10, Halley was nearly three times farther away than at its minimum distance in 1910. And it had arrived at this point a full two months after perihelion (instead of two weeks as in 1910) — long after its brightest phase had passed. Even those living or traveling to the Southern Hemisphere (as I did), where the comet was well placed, didn't witness a true showstopper. To make matters worse, Halley's tail suddenly ebbed at the beginning of April, leaving behind a small, condensed, nebulous mass with a stubby, fan-shaped appendage.

The leviathan turned out to be a mere tadpole!

A scientific gold mine

But while Halley disappointed the public, it proved to be an astronomical gold mine for astronomers. Within three weeks in March 1986, an international armada of spacecraft studied the comet: Japan launched Sakigake and Suisei; the Soviet Union sent VEGA 1 and VEGA 2; NASA contributed the International Cometary Explorer (ICE); and the European Space Agency, then a consortium of 11 countries, launched Giotto.

VEGA 1 and 2 and Giotto plunged deep into Halley's coma — the fuzzy, glowing cloud of gas and dust that surrounds the nucleus when it travels close to the sun — and revealed it to be an active, sputtering mass that responds violently to heating by the sun. Jets of dust were expelled from the nucleus with explosive intensity. And we discovered that the nucleus is encrusted in a dark shroud of its own debris and is as black as coal or velvet. Each VEGA spacecraft came to within about 5,300 miles (8,500 km) of Halley.

Giotto passed within just 375 miles (600 km) of the nucleus. More than 2,000 returned images showed that Halley's nucleus was larger than expected and shaped like a peanut or potato, measuring 9 miles (14 km) long and 5 miles (8 km) wide. The nucleus spins on its longest axis every 7.4 days, while the entire body appears to wobble in half that time. The images also revealed three "active regions," areas where volatile gases and dust escape when sunlight heats the surface. As the comet rotates, fresh ice enters the sunlight and sublimates; the escaping gas then drags entrained dust particles away from the nucleus.

Surprises beyond 1986

Long after 1986, a receding Halley's Comet showed that it could still provide some surprises. On Feb. 12, 1991, between the orbits of Saturn and Uranus at 1.329 billion miles (2.138 billion km) from the sun, Halley was photographed from the European Southern Observatory in Chile by two Belgian astronomers. They had expected to find the comet appearing as nothing more than a faint speck of light. Instead, it appeared as a monstrous nebula 300 times brighter than expected; a massive outburst.

The cause of the dramatic flare-up remains a mystery. An unknown body may have collided with the comet. Another possibility is that the nucleus released a large amount of latent internal energy, although such a release would be unlikely so far from the sun. Highly energetic particles in the solar wind may also have reached the comet in sufficient numbers to heat its surface.

The road to 2061

On Dec. 8, 2023, Halley's Comet reached aphelion; the farthest point in its orbit from the sun.

Halley is expected to return in the summer of 2061, in circumstances that will largely mirror those of 1986 — but with one crucial difference. This time the comet will be fully visible on the same side of the sun as Earth and should appear at least 10 times brighter. In the morning sky, it will reach its northernmost position on July 24. It will then move rapidly southward as it enters the evening sky, gradually favoring more southerly locations. Even so, viewers at mid-northern latitudes should see an eye-catching object low in the west-northwest sky in early August.

And we don't have to wait until 2061 to experience Halley.

Like all comets, Halley's is a cosmic litterbug and, as such, it leaves behind in its wake a trail of — for lack of a better term — garbage, composed of tiny bits and crumbs of space debris that can produce beautiful incandescent trails upon impacting our atmosphere. Because they emanate from the constellation Orion, we call them the Orionid meteors, which will reach their peak on Oct. 21.

In a way, I guess you can call them "rock stars," but eventually, they fall down to Earth.

Joe Rao serves as an instructor and guest lecturer at New York's Hayden Planetarium. He writes about astronomy for Natural History magazine, Sky and Telescope, The Old Farmer's Almanac and other publications.

On Feb. 12, 1991, between the orbits of Saturn and Uranus at 1.329 billion miles (2.138 billion km) from the sun, Halley was photographed from the European Southern Observatory in Chile by two Belgian astronomers. They had expected to find the comet appearing as nothing more than a faint speck of light. Instead, it appeared as a monstrous nebula 300 times brighter than expected; a massive outburst.

The cause of the dramatic flare-up remains a mystery. An unknown body may have collided with the comet. Another possibility is that the nucleus released a large amount of latent internal energy, although such a release would be unlikely so far from the sun. Highly energetic particles in the solar wind may also have reached the comet in sufficient numbers to heat its surface.

The road to 2061

On Dec. 8, 2023, Halley's Comet reached aphelion; the farthest point in its orbit from the sun.

Halley is expected to return in the summer of 2061, in circumstances that will largely mirror those of 1986 — but with one crucial difference. This time the comet will be fully visible on the same side of the sun as Earth and should appear at least 10 times brighter. In the morning sky, it will reach its northernmost position on July 24. It will then move rapidly southward as it enters the evening sky, gradually favoring more southerly locations. Even so, viewers at mid-northern latitudes should see an eye-catching object low in the west-northwest sky in early August.

And we don't have to wait until 2061 to experience Halley.

Like all comets, Halley's is a cosmic litterbug and, as such, it leaves behind in its wake a trail of — for lack of a better term — garbage, composed of tiny bits and crumbs of space debris that can produce beautiful incandescent trails upon impacting our atmosphere. Because they emanate from the constellation Orion, we call them the Orionid meteors, which will reach their peak on Oct. 21.

In a way, I guess you can call them "rock stars," but eventually, they fall down to Earth.

]]> <![CDATA[ A faint glow from the early universe could help solve the mystery of dark energy ]]> Hydrogen may be the most common element in the cosmos, but scientists could use it to do something unique: uncover the nature of dark energy, the mysterious force driving the accelerating expansion of the universe.

This new line of dark energy investigation comes from the fact that researchers have determined that the CHIME (Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment) project can detect the faint radio glow of hydrogen from the universe's distant past.

Not only does this represent a faster and much less expensive way to investigate dark energy, but it is a major milestone for CHIME. The instrument was specifically devised to investigate dark energy and its pervasive influence.

"This is a completely new technique for probing the cosmos, delivered by an instrument that was conceived and built by Canadians," CHIME principal investigator Mark Halpern of the University of British Columbia said in a statement. "It's a bold new step in the global cosmology program and a Canadian success story."

Why is dark energy so problematic?

Dark energy is the mysterious force that is accelerating the expansion of the universe. It is so problematic for scientists because it started acting on the fabric of space only after the expansion triggered by the Big Bang had halted.

That's akin to pushing a child on a swing, watching it stop, and then seeing the swing start up again without a push. And, not only that, but the swing starts oscillating faster and faster. Consider scientists akin to very worried parents, who would really like to know where this ghostly push came from and how it is going to proceed.

Just as, if the push on the swing continues, the child could end up in the bushes, or in orbit, the strengthening of dark energy could result in the cold death of the cosmos, or even a "Big Rip" scenario that sees space shredded. Alternatively, if it weakens and allows gravity to reassert dominance, then the universe could collapse back in on itself, resulting in a "Big Crunch" ending that sees the cosmos compressed back into a singularity, as it was at the beginning of time.

Dark energy is now the dominant element of the universe, accounting for 68% of the universe's matter-energy budget. It's little wonder that scientists are very keen to know what this mysterious force is.

So how can hydrogen help the investigation of dark energy?

"Hydrogen is the most common element in the universe and the raw material from which stars form," team member Arnab Chakraborty of the University of Toronto said. "Its faint radio emission acts like a cosmic tracer, revealing how matter is distributed across space."

Previously, CHIME could map the distribution of hydrogen in the early universe but only by cross-correlating its observations with galaxy survey data from other telescopes, operations that cost millions of dollars and can only focus on regions of the universe dense enough to form stars. CHIME has now shown it can map the radio glow of hydrogen all on its own.

Indeed, the team has already begun making steps in this direction using just a tiny fraction of existing CHIME data. Using 94 nights of observations from 2019, they detected a hydrogen signal from when the universe was just 5 billion years old.

"Our data indicate that roughly 2% of the hydrogen in the universe was in neutral atomic form at this time, broadly consistent with other measurements," team member Shabbir Shaikh of Arizona State University said. "By measuring how that hydrogen is distributed and clustered, CHIME gives us a new way to test our understanding of how galaxies form and evolve."

CHIME has now collected seven years of data, and using this, the team is hoping to probe the distribution of hydrogen back to 3 billion years after the Big Bang.

The team's research was published across two papers in The Astrophysical Journal.

]]> <![CDATA[ SpaceX launches Falcon 9 Starlink mission for 1st time in more than 3 weeks (video) ]]>

SpaceX just broke an uncharacteristically long Starlink launch drought.

The company sent 27 of its Starlink internet satellites to low Earth orbit (LEO) today (Oct. 12), launching them atop a Falcon 9 rocket from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base at 8:28 p.m. EDT (5:28 p.m. local time; 0028 GMT on Oct. 13)

It was the first Starlink mission for a Falcon 9 since Sept. 19, which was another 27-satellite liftoff from Vandenberg. For some perspective on this recent gap: Between Aug. 19 and Sept. 6, a span of 19 days, SpaceX launched seven Starlink missions with Falcon 9s.

SpaceX did loft a batch of Starlinks after that, but it wasn't aboard a Falcon 9. The company's Starship megarocket carried 26 next-gen Starlink V3 craft on its 14th test flight, which took place on Sept. 28.

Starship reached orbit for the first time ever on Flight 14, and it deployed the Starlinks successfully as well. This will happen many more times going forward, if all goes to plan: The Starlink V3 constellation will eventually consist of about 100,000 satellites, all of which will fly on Starship, Elon Musk has said.

Indeed, SpaceX plans to sunset the Falcon 9 and its cousin, the Falcon Heavy, in the next few years, shifting their duties over to the fully reusable, far more powerful Starship, which remains in the test-flight phase.

That shift will be a big one for the spaceflight community, for the Falcon 9 is the workhorse rocket of its generation. In 2025, for example, it flew 165 times — roughly the same number as the rest of the world's orbital launchers combined. Nearly three-quarters of those Falcon 9 launches were Starlink missions.

Things have slowed down a bit in 2026. Today's flight was the 112th Falcon 9 liftoff of the year, and the 82nd in service of the Starlink megaconstellation, which currently consists of more than 11,100 active satellites.

Previous Booster 1088 launches

NROL-126 | Transporter-12 | SPHEREx | NROL-57 | USSF-366 | 14 Starlink missions

All went according to plan on today's launch. The Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth as planned, touching down about 8.5 minutes after launch on the drone ship "Of Course I Still Love You," which was stationed in the Pacific Ocean. It was the 20th launch and landing for this particular booster, which is designated B1088.

The rocket's expendable upper stage, meanwhile, delivered the 27 spacecraft to LEO, deploying them there 62 minutes after liftoff, SpaceX announced via X.

]]> <![CDATA[ SpaceX successfully launches 6,300 pounds of cargo to the International Space Station ]]>

SpaceX launched its latest cargo mission to the International Space Station (ISS) on Tuesday morning (Oct. 13).

A Falcon 9 rocket launched a robotic Dragon capsule to the orbiting lab from Florida's Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Tuesday at 6:35 a.m. EDT (1035 GMT).

The launch kicks off the CRS-35 mission, so named because it will be the 35th that SpaceX flies under a Commercial Resupply Services contract with NASA.

If all goes according to plan, Dragon will reach the International Space Station (ISS) on Thursday (Oct. 15), docking autonomously to the space-facing port of its Harmony module at around 11 a.m. EDT (1500 GMT). You can watch the arrival here at Space.com as well; coverage will start at 9:15 a.m. EDT (1315 GMT).

CRS-35 will deliver 6,300 pounds (2,860 kilograms) of supplies to the astronauts aboard the orbiting lab, including the final set of International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Arrays (iROSAs), which will boost the orbiting lab's energy budget.

There's also quite a bit of scientific gear heading up on the flight.

Dragon "will deliver hardware to manufacture artificial retinas in microgravity to help restore vision on Earth and 3D heart tissue models to advance large‑scale drug testing on future missions," NASA officials wrote in a CRS-35 launch preview on Oct. 7.

"The spacecraft will carry materials to study how a new type of glass forms in microgravity and brain organoids that could reveal treatment targets for neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and multiple sclerosis," they added.

Dragon will stay attached to the ISS for about a month, then head back down to Earth with scientific experiments and other hardware. It will splash down safely under parachutes in the Pacific Ocean off the California coast.

SpaceX's Dragon is the only currently operational freighter that can carry cargo in the downward direction. The other three — Russia's Progress, Japan's HTV-X and Northrop Grumman's Cygnus XL — are all expendable, burning up in Earth's atmosphere after their time at the ISS is done.

Editor's note: This story was updated at 6:59 a.m. EDT on Oct. 13 with news of a successful launch.

]]> <![CDATA[ Astronomers witness supermassive black hole gorge on a cosmic meal before 'burping' radio jets 300 days later ]]> Using the NASA X-ray spacecraft Swift combined with radio observations, astronomers have observed a supermassive black hole burping radio jets 300 days after a heavy cosmic meal. The team was also able to roughly estimate the mass of this feeding cosmic titan, which sits at the heart of the Perseus Cluster, a massive collection of thousands of galaxies.

The black hole sits at the center of the galaxy NGC 1275, located around 225 light-years away, and is the brightest galaxy of the Perseus Cluster. The supermassive black hole first flared in X-rays, which indicated an increase in the rate at which it was accreting matter. Actively feeding supermassive black holes sit in regions called active galactic nuclei (AGNs), with their immense gravity heating surrounding matter, causing them to glow brightly. These emissions are boosted by material channeled to the poles of the central black hole, from where it is blasted out as powerful twin jets that shine across the electromagnetic spectrum, particularly in radio waves.

The observation of the following radio jet from the AGN at the heart of NGC 1275 via flaring in radio waves is crucial for understanding the relationship between the disk of matter that surrounds and feeds the black hole, called an accretion disk, and the jets it launches. This so-called disk-jet coupling is key to developing a better picture of how black holes influence star formation in the galaxies in which they sit, and thus the growth of those galaxies.

Making these observations is no mean feat. The ideal spacecraft for observing X-ray emissions is Chandra, but it doesn't observe NGC 1275 frequently enough to observe its long-term behaviour. NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory may lack the power of Chandra, but having launched in 2004, it has collected a vast amount of data regarding NGC 1275 and its central supermassive black hole.

"It is fairly difficult to see the inner region of this AGN because NGC 1275 is at the center of the massive Perseus cluster of galaxies, which adds additional light to our observations," team leader Sarah Ketchum of the University of Michigan told Space.com. "We developed a model that allowed us to remove the cluster emission from archival Swift data, and in doing so, we were able to see the changes in the X-ray flux from gas accreting onto the black hole in NGC 1275, from 2007 to 2025."

Ketchum added that the capabilities of Swift were key to this investigation of NGC 1275, which is the ideal laboratory for the study of disk-jet coupling.

"There have been studies on other galaxies with AGN that show evidence of coupling between gas accretion traced in X-ray light and gas ejection in jets, traced in radio light. But NGC 1275 reveals the impact of black hole jets on large spatial scales better than any other system," the University of Michigan researcher continued.

This black hole didn't eat a star

Ketchum and colleagues saw the strongest ever X-ray flare from NGC 1275 in Feb. 2023. Lasting less than 60 days and consisting of two 5-day blasts, this episode saw a doubling of the X-ray brightness of the AGN at the heart of NGC 1275.

The flaring was so extreme that the team had to rule out a tidal disruption event (TDE) as the cause. These occur when an unfortunate star's orbit brings it too close to the immense gravitational influence of a supermassive black hole. This influence generates intense tidal forces that simultaneously squash and squeeze the star, "speghettifying" it and allowing the black hole to snack on some plasma pasta.

"We were able to rule out TDEs as a cause," Ketchum said. "Thus, the flaring was likely caused by a spike in the rate at which matter accreted onto the black hole."

Using Swift data, the team was able to infer the radius over which the AGN emits radiation. Because the size of a black hole is directly correlated with its mass, this meant that the researchers were able to constrain the mass of the black hole at the heart of NGC 1275. They determined that this supermassive black hole has a mass somewhere between 100 million times the mass of the sun and 1 billion solar masses.

The team then compared their data to known radio data to better understand the relationship between the X-ray emission and the radio jets that disrupt gas in NGC 1275.

Ketchum added that she and her colleagues found tentative evidence of around a 300-day delay between the X-ray flaring and the radio wave emission. This indicates the time it takes plasma to travel from the base of the jet to a knot or shock created when it hits surrounding gas or dust.

"This should be tested further in the future. Our X-ray data only sparsely sample the changes in NGC 1275," Ketchum said. "This makes it difficult to determine an exact relationship between the X-ray and radio radiation for large portions of our light curve, so we would need more X-ray data to further study this connection."

The researcher added that if the X-ray flares are produced close to the black hole, an echo of these flares should be seen coming from the accretion disk.

"An emission line from neutral iron is seen in data from NGC 1275, and this may be the echo. However, we likely need many observations with XMM-Newton and XRISM ( X-Ray Imaging and Spectroscopy Mission) to really establish that connection," Ketchum concluded.

The team's research has been accepted for publication in the Astrophysical Journal Letters, with a pre-peer-review version available on the repository site arXiv.

]]> <![CDATA[ The moon could turn astronauts into 'walking, high voltage capacitors' that accidentally zap spacecraft ]]> NASA is asking for ideas to stop static electricity from zapping astronauts or critical hardware during moon missions.

The agency opened a "Lunar Grounding Challenge" to avoid situations where an astronaut on the moon could become "a walking, high voltage capacitor." Submissions for the $150,000 competition are due Jan. 15 and you can see the requirements here.

NASA is hoping to put astronaut boots at the lunar south pole in 2028 during the Artemis 4 or 5 missions, on the first landing mission since NASA's Apollo 17 in 1972. But simulations suggest that both "tribocharging" (electric-charge transfer between two objects) and plasma charging (from ambient gas in the region) could build up electric charge on spacesuits. "This problem is severely compounded when entering lunar shadows and permanently shadowed regions," the agency wrote, referring to deeply cratered areas where the sun does not touch the lunar surface.

The concern is that astronauts' spacesuits could become electrically charged, as there would be an excess of electrons (negatively charged particles) compared with ions (positively charged) in these areas.

"The risk occurs when an astronaut returns to the spacecraft," the agency added. The lander would have a slight positive charge, producing an issue once the "highly negatively-charged astronaut approaches the vehicle."

NASA has asked industry partners for ideas that can help an astronaut avoid "becoming a walking, high voltage capacitor", including issues such as an electrical arc that could damage spacesuits, spark fires in the oxygen atmosphere of a spacecraft, or create electrical shocks. (A Mars simulation in 2018 was reportedly derailed due to a crew experiencing electrical issues, so this problem is not unprecedented.)

The challenge aims to create designs that would safely discharge the astronaut and their spacesuit before an astronaut touches the lander. Among the technical requirements, NASA is looking for something small (in terms of mass, volume and power) that would be able to operate even in the extreme temperature swings of the lunar surface. The technology must also be able to help as many as four extra-vehicular activities (moonwalks) that take place over as long as 10 days.

"In addition, the suspended lunar dust and heavy dust buildup on a suit in these environments significantly increases arcing lengths, allowing sparks to jump across larger gaps than they would in a clean vacuum. Therefore, the solution must aim to avoid a sudden arc that may come into contact with the outer pressure garment — suit — or the lander," NASA wrote in the challenge description.

The challenge will include multiple phases, including a concept design, concept refinement after chatting with reviewers, and then a final selection. NASA did not release a target date in its press release for when the tech would be available for astronauts, but the agency is planning on a long-term moon base for astronaut missions that would be largely ready to go in the 2030s if schedules hold.

]]> https://www.space.com/astronomy/moon/the-moon-could-turn-astronauts-into-walking-high-voltage-capacitors-that-accidentally-zap-spacecraft 8VkQfuMUAPhoApbUde3R8j Mon, 12 Oct 2026 18:00:00 +0000 Tue, 13 Oct 2026 07:17:46 +0000 false false false

NASA is asking for ideas to stop static electricity from zapping astronauts or critical hardware during moon missions.

The agency opened a "Lunar Grounding Challenge" to avoid situations where an astronaut on the moon could become "a walking, high voltage capacitor." Submissions for the $150,000 competition are due Jan. 15 and you can see the requirements here.

NASA is hoping to put astronaut boots at the lunar south pole in 2028 during the Artemis 4 or 5 missions, on the first landing mission since NASA's Apollo 17 in 1972. But simulations suggest that both "tribocharging" (electric-charge transfer between two objects) and plasma charging (from ambient gas in the region) could build up electric charge on spacesuits. "This problem is severely compounded when entering lunar shadows and permanently shadowed regions," the agency wrote, referring to deeply cratered areas where the sun does not touch the lunar surface.

The concern is that astronauts' spacesuits could become electrically charged, as there would be an excess of electrons (negatively charged particles) compared with ions (positively charged) in these areas.

"The risk occurs when an astronaut returns to the spacecraft," the agency added. The lander would have a slight positive charge, producing an issue once the "highly negatively-charged astronaut approaches the vehicle."

NASA has asked industry partners for ideas that can help an astronaut avoid "becoming a walking, high voltage capacitor", including issues such as an electrical arc that could damage spacesuits, spark fires in the oxygen atmosphere of a spacecraft, or create electrical shocks. (A Mars simulation in 2018 was reportedly derailed due to a crew experiencing electrical issues, so this problem is not unprecedented.)

The challenge aims to create designs that would safely discharge the astronaut and their spacesuit before an astronaut touches the lander. Among the technical requirements, NASA is looking for something small (in terms of mass, volume and power) that would be able to operate even in the extreme temperature swings of the lunar surface. The technology must also be able to help as many as four extra-vehicular activities (moonwalks) that take place over as long as 10 days.

"In addition, the suspended lunar dust and heavy dust buildup on a suit in these environments significantly increases arcing lengths, allowing sparks to jump across larger gaps than they would in a clean vacuum. Therefore, the solution must aim to avoid a sudden arc that may come into contact with the outer pressure garment — suit — or the lander," NASA wrote in the challenge description.

The challenge will include multiple phases, including a concept design, concept refinement after chatting with reviewers, and then a final selection. NASA did not release a target date in its press release for when the tech would be available for astronauts, but the agency is planning on a long-term moon base for astronaut missions that would be largely ready to go in the 2030s if schedules hold.

    <item>
      <title>Koalice prosadila mimořádné jednání o cestě prezidenta Pavla do Maroka</title>
      <link>https://www.idnes.cz/zpravy/domaci/koalice-prosadila-mimoradne-jednani-o-ceste-prezidenta-pavla-do-maroka.A261013_175936_domaci_kop#utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=zpravodaj&utm_content=main</link>
      <description>Poslanci vládní koalice ANO, SPD, Motoristé sobě prosadili do programu jednání výzvu Poslanecké sněmovny prezidentovi Petru Pavlovi, aby zveřejnil informace o financování své soukromé dovolené v Maroku. Navrhl to poslanec SPD, předseda strany PRO Jindřich Rajchl.</description>
      <pubDate>Tue, 13 Oct 2026 16:09:00 GMT</pubDate>
      <category domain="https://www.idnes.cz/zpravy/domaci">Zprávy - Domácí</category>
      <comments>https://www.idnes.cz/zpravy/domaci/koalice-prosadila-mimoradne-jednani-o-ceste-prezidenta-pavla-do-maroka.A261013_175936_domaci_kop/diskuse</comments>
      <guid isPermaLink="false">A261013_175936_domaci_kop</guid>
      <media:content url="https://1gr.cz/fotky/idnes/26/101/cl6/MIKb2964d82e5_pavel.jpg" type="image/jpeg" />
      <media:description>„Kamarád z Dakaru Petr Pavel nás navštívil i na Rallye du Maroc. Děkujeme!“ napsal automobilový jezdec Martin Prokop na svém facebooku. (2. října 2026)</media:description>
      <media:credit>Martin Prokop - Facebook</media:credit>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Poradní tým dětského ombudsmana odmítá plošný zákaz mobilů na školách</title>
      <link>https://www.idnes.cz/zpravy/domaci/poradni-tym-detskeho-ombudsmana-kritizuje-zakaz-mobilu-skoly.A261013_175617_domaci_sahu#utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=zpravodaj&utm_content=main</link>
      <description>Žádný ze členů poradního týmu dětského ombudsmana nesouhlasí s chystaným plošným zákazem používání mobilních telefonů ve školách. Zástupci dětí vytýkají zákonodárcům chybějící diskusi s těmi, kterých se změna přímo dotýká, a upozorňují na nedostatečnou osvětu o rizicích a zdravém používání digitálních technologií. Kancelář ombudsmana a dětského ombudsmana o tom v úterý informovala na webu.</description>
      <pubDate>Tue, 13 Oct 2026 16:07:00 GMT</pubDate>
      <category domain="https://www.idnes.cz/zpravy/domaci">Zprávy - Domácí</category>

      <media:credit>Shutterstock</media:credit>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Poslanci jednají o dani pro rafinerie. Nezvýší ceny, ujišťuje Schillerová</title>
      <link>https://www.idnes.cz/zpravy/domaci/snemovna-mimoradne-zdaneni-narustu-marzi-rafinerii-vlada.A261013_050128_domaci_kop#utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=zpravodaj&utm_content=main</link>
      <description>Poslanci projednávají návrh vlády Andreje Babiše na zavedení mimořádné daně pro rafinerie pro letošní a příští rok. Vláda ho zdůvodňuje růstem marží rafinerií kvůli situaci na světovém trhu s ropou. „Téma rezonuje na evropské úrovni,“ řekla ministryně financí Alena Schillerová. Změna se podle ní nepromítne do cen pro spotřebitele.</description>

    <item>
      <title>Osm let stačilo, dejte to bez ANO. Ve Zlíně sílí nespokojenost s chystanou koalicí</title>
      <link>https://www.idnes.cz/volby/zlin/komunalni-volby-2026-zlin-ods-povolebni-vyjednavani.A261013_170053_zlin-volby_jfuk#utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=zpravodaj&utm_content=main</link>
      <description>Povolební vyjednávání o nové koalici ve Zlíně pokračují. Situace se vyvíjí také v jednotlivých stranách, které by ji mohly společně s vítězným ANO sestavit. Poté, co se ozvaly nespokojené hlasy voličů proti účasti hnutí Zlín 21, které před volbami slibovalo změnu, zní negativní vyjádření také z tábora ODS.</description>

      <media:description>Lídr ODS Miroslav Chalánek zdraví lídra ANO, primátora Jiřího Korce. (10. říjen 2026)</media:description>

    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Čtyři roky je kritizovali, teď s ODS a ANO domluvili koalici. Zrada, zní od voličů</title>
      <link>https://www.idnes.cz/volby/zlin/komunalni-volby-2026-uherske-hradiste-hradistaci-koalice-ods-ano.A261013_080645_zlin-volby_jfuk#utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=zpravodaj&utm_content=main</link>
      <description>Je to ten nejméně očekávaný výsledek povolebního vyjednávání v Uherském Hradišti. V pondělí večer se na koaliční spolupráci dohodlo vítězné hnutí Hradišťáci se zástupci ANO a ODS. Tedy stranami, které hnutí čtyři roky z opozice kritizovalo. Dlouholetý starosta Stanislav Blaha tak zůstává součástí vedení radnice. Jeho nástupcem by se měl stát lídr Hradišťáků Michal Dvouletý.  </description>
      <pubDate>Tue, 13 Oct 2026 15:51:00 GMT</pubDate>
      <category domain="https://www.idnes.cz/volby/zlin">Zlín - Zlín - Volby</category>

      <media:description>Vítězné hnutí Hradišťáci složilo koalici s ANO a ODS. V popředí zleva: Stanislav Blaha (ODS), Michal Dvouletý (Hradišťáci) a Jana Grygarová (ANO). (říjen 2026)</media:description>
      <media:credit>Hradišťáci</media:credit>
    </item>
    <item>

      <link>https://www.idnes.cz/volby/do-politiky-se-hrnou-tisice-lidi-s-titulem-mudr-jejich-sance-uspet-ale-klesaji.A261013_162906_domaci_ichuc#utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=zpravodaj&utm_content=main</link>
      <description>Bílý plášť a titul MUDr. byly dříve silnou značkou i pro politiku. Nejméně každý třetí doktor, který chtěl mandát, uspěl. Lidé je často volili, i když je neznali. Věřili jim kvůli profesi. Když v roce 2002 kandidovalo do měst a obcí 3 104 lékařů, místo v zastupitelstvu získalo 38 procent z nich. Letos jich kandidovalo o 700 méně, ale většina se dočkala ledové sprchy. Je zřejmé, že jen titul už nestačí.</description>

    <item>
      <title>Jako záchranář vidím, co lidi trápí, říká Vašica před druhým kolem voleb</title>
      <link>https://www.idnes.cz/volby/zlin/senatni-volby-2026-uherske-hradiste-vasica-ano-rozhovor.A261013_976773_zlin-zpravy_jfuk#utm_source=rss&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=zpravodaj&utm_content=main</link>
      <description>Do finálového souboje senátních voleb v Uherském Hradišti postoupil jako druhý Jiří Vašica (ANO). O místo v Senátu usiluje z pozice radního v Uherském Hradišti. Pracuje 26 let jako záchranář, proto by se v případě úspěchu chtěl věnovat dostupnosti zdravotní péče, zdravému životnímu stylu nebo sociálnímu bydlení.	</description>

      <description>Umělá inteligence by se už během několika měsíců mohla sama kopírovat a šířit mezi chytrými televizemi, lednicemi nebo dalšími spotřebiči připojenými k internetu.       <description>Současná ruská agrese proti Ukrajině devastuje ruské regiony v dosud nevídaném měřítku. Ruský publicista Alexandr Chramov na svém blogu analyzoval lokální památník padlých, který bez příkras ukazuje reálnou cenu, jakou ruská společnost platí za imperiální ambice Kremlu.</description>

      <media:content url="https://1gr.cz/fotky/idnes/26/102/cl6/REM8eecb756e6_photo_2026_10_11_09_14_28.jpg" type="image/jpeg" />
      <media:description>Ruský publicista Alexandr Chramov analyzoval památník padlých v městě Arzamas v Nižněnovgordské oblasti. Ukazuje se, že současné tažení na Ukrajinu zlikvidovalo v tomto regionu patnáctkrát více mužů než obě čečenské války a sovětská okupace Afghánistánu dohromady.</media:description>

<link>https://www.lupa.cz/aktuality/cesti-vedci-vyvijeji-s-lockheed-martin-umelou-inteligenci-ktera-z-reci-pozna-pretizeneho-pilota/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=text&utm_campaign=rss</link>
<description>Če&#353;tí vědci z Fakulty informačních technologií VUT v Brně spolupracují s americkým gigantem Lockheed Martin na vývoji umělé inteligence, která má rozpoznat, kdy je vojenský pilot pod nebezpečným tlakem. Systém analyzuje změny v jeho hlase a porovnává je s údaji o fyzickém stavu získanými z dal&#353;ích senzorů. Cílem je odhalit kognitivní přetížení dřív, než takový stav ohrozí pilota nebo letadlo.</description>

<description>České Radiokomunikace (CRA) od leto&#353;ního listopadu reorganizují svůj stále rostoucí a důležitěj&#353;í byznys s datovými centry, cloudem a provozem serverů.  <description>Americká velvyslankyně v Řecku Kimberly Guilfoyleová končí ve funkci.  <description>Počet potvrzených případů eboly v Kongu vzrostl na 9066, včetně 4381 úmrtí. Podle agentury Reuters to vyplývá z v úterý zveřejněných údajů konžského institutu veřejného zdraví.  <description>Maďarští poslanci v úterý odhlasovali zrušení právních ustanovení proti LGBT+ komunitě. Pro se vyslovilo 139 z nich, 59 hlasovalo proti, informovala agentura AFP. <description>Če&#353;tí vědci z Fakulty informačních technologií VUT v Brně spolupracují s americkým gigantem Lockheed Martin na vývoji umělé inteligence, která má rozpoznat, kdy je vojenský pilot pod nebezpečným tlakem. Kudy z nudy – Žebříčky: Liberecký kraj Žebříčky RSS Feed <![CDATA[Šťastné a křišťálové – Vánoce naruby]]>

Přijďte prožít advent do libereckého Paláce Liebieg, kde se letos potkají tradice, kreativita a vánoční atmosféra Křišťálového údolí. Čeká vás jedinečná výstava, která vás zavede do světa fantazie, kde nic není takové, jak se na první pohled zdá.

]]> Fri, 09 Oct 2026 15:54:49 GMT <![CDATA[Židovská modlitebna a synagoga Liberec]]>

Novodobá liberecká synagoga je součástí Krajské vědecké knihovny, známé jako Stavba smíření. Otevřena byla roku 2000 na místě synagogy vypálené nacisty. Trojúhelníkový půdorys připomíná část Davidovy hvězdy a interiér uchovává památky původního svatostánku.

]]> Fri, 09 Oct 2026 11:36:28 GMT <![CDATA[Kostel sv. Vojtěcha v Liberci]]>

Kostel sv. Vojtěcha v libereckém Ostašově stojí na místě dřevěné kaple vybudované z odškodnění za sedmiletou válku. Zděná stavba vznikla v letech 1832–1833. Díky péči Spolku přátel Ostašova dnes ožívá koncerty a dalšími kulturními akcemi.

]]> Fri, 09 Oct 2026 11:29:30 GMT <![CDATA[Kostel sv. Jana Křtitele v Liberci]]>

Barokní kostel sv. Jana Křtitele v liberecké Rochlici stojí na místě někdejšího dřevěného evangelického kostela. Zaujme dochovaným historickým vybavením, hlavním oltářem s obrazem patrona chrámu, vyřezávanou kazatelnou a varhanami z roku 1887.

]]> Fri, 09 Oct 2026 11:23:32 GMT

Chodec přes veškerou snahu záchranářů na místě svému zranění podlehl.</description></item><item><title>Areál bývalého sanatoria v Machníně ožil. Začala stavba Alzheimer centra</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/902894-areal-byvaleho-sanatoria-v-machnine-ozil-zacala-stavba-alzheimer-centra.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/902894-areal-byvaleho-sanatoria-v-machnine-ozil-zacala-stavba-alzheimer-centra.html</guid><pubDate>Tue, 13 Oct 2026 13:21:00 +0200</pubDate><dc:creator>Luboš Vrabec</dc:creator><category>Společnost</category><description>Dlouhé roky areál bývalého očního sanatoria v libereckém Machníně chátral. To se nakonec podařilo a developer Dolcevita zde vybuduje Alzheimer centrum a v další etapě domov pro seniory.</description></item><item><title>V Jablonci po volbách bez výraznější změny. Koalice pokračuje, ANO je v opozici</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/politika/902889-v-jablonci-po-volbach-bez-vyraznejsi-zmeny-koalice-pokracuje-ano-je-v-opozici.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/politika/902889-v-jablonci-po-volbach-bez-vyraznejsi-zmeny-koalice-pokracuje-ano-je-v-opozici.html</guid><pubDate>Tue, 13 Oct 2026 12:00:00 +0200</pubDate><dc:creator>Martina Petrášková</dc:creator><category>Politika</category><description>Jablonec nad Nisou povede v příštích čtyřech letech koalice složená ze zástupců Starostů pro Liberecký kraj, ODS, Společně pro Jablonec a Pirátů a nezávislých. Primátorem zůstane Miloš Vele z ODS. Vítěz voleb ANO zůstává v opozici.</description></item><item><title>Vesecký areál zaplavily stovky školáků. Konal se okresní přebor v přespolním běhu</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/sport/902857-vesecky-areal-zaplavily-stovky-skolaku-konal-se-okresni-prebor-v-prespolnim-behu.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/sport/902857-vesecky-areal-zaplavily-stovky-skolaku-konal-se-okresni-prebor-v-prespolnim-behu.html</guid><pubDate>Tue, 13 Oct 2026 10:56:00 +0200</pubDate><dc:creator>Luboš Vrabec</dc:creator><category>Sport</category><description>Téměř čtyři stovky mladých sportovců ze základních a středních škol Liberecka změřily síly na tradičním Okresním kole v přespolním běhu. Slavnostně bude otevřena ve středu 28. října v 10 hodin. Už teď ale funguje ve zkušebním provozu a je přístupná.</description></item><item><title>Dvě nedělní nehody na Jablonecku: Zatáčky vynesly řidiče do patníku i protisměru</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/doprava/902804-dve-nedelni-nehody-na-jablonecku-zatacky-vynesly-ridice-do-patniku-i-protismeru.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/doprava/902804-dve-nedelni-nehody-na-jablonecku-zatacky-vynesly-ridice-do-patniku-i-protismeru.html</guid><pubDate>Mon, 12 Oct 2026 19:28:00 +0200</pubDate><dc:creator>Martina Petrášková</dc:creator><category>Doprava</category><description>Neděle na Jablonecku se neobešla bez nehod na silnicích. Dva řidiči doplatili na neopatrnost v levotočivých zatáčkách – jeden skončil v protisměru a způsobil zranění druhého šoféra, další se svým vozem narazil čelně do kamenného patníku. Alkohol byl u obou vyloučen.</description></item><item><title>Příprava na zimu na Ještědu začíná: Unikátní technologie chrlí tuny ledu denně</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/902811-priprava-na-zimu-na-jestedu-zacina-unikatni-technologie-chrli-tuny-ledu-denne.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/spolecnost/902811-priprava-na-zimu-na-jestedu-zacina-unikatni-technologie-chrli-tuny-ledu-denne.html</guid><pubDate>Mon, 12 Oct 2026 18:00:00 +0200</pubDate><dc:creator>Martina Petrášková</dc:creator><category>Společnost</category><description>Skiareál Ještěd se intenzivně připravuje na zimní sezónu a znovu sází na technologii Snow Factory. Unikátní metoda bez použití chemie vytvoří pevný základ na kritických úsecích sjezdovek a výrazně urychlí zahájení lyžování.</description></item><item><title>Proč nesmí děti cestovat v bundě? Tohle se stane při nehodě</title><link>https://liberecka.drbna.cz/doprava/902440-proc-nesmi-deti-cestovat-v-bunde-tohle-se-stane-pri-nehode.html</link><guid isPermaLink="true">https://liberecka.drbna.cz/doprava/902440-proc-nesmi-deti-cestovat-v-bunde-tohle-se-stane-pri-nehode.html</guid><pubDate>Mon, 12 Oct 2026 16:41:00 +0200</pubDate><category>Doprava</category><description>Péřovka v autosedačce může být při nehodě stejně nebezpečná jako nezapnutý pás.
